Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:65: Therefore it is fitting for a person to resemble his Creator, just as they said (Berachot 58b; Tikkunei Zohar 1b), it is enough for a servant to be like his master; and just as in exile our Father suffers with our suffering, as it is said (Isaiah 63:9), "in all their affliction, He was afflicted" — and "lo tzar" [not/for Him it was distress] is explained not as "not distress" but "for Him distress," that the distress reached even to the supernal letter, as explained in the Bahir and likewise in the Zohar, portion Vayera (120b) — so it is fitting for a person to suffer likewise.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:66: And just as He weeps, as it is written (Jeremiah 13:17), "in secret places my soul shall weep because of pride," and it is explained in tractate Chagigah (5b) that the Holy One, blessed be He, has a place where He weeps, called "Mistarim" [secret places] — so should a person weep.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:67: And just as from the day the Temple was destroyed there is no laughter before Him, as we learn in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah (3b): Rav Acha of Migdal said to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, since the Temple was destroyed, there is no laughter before the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said (Isaiah 42:14), "I have kept silent from of old" — so it is not fitting that his mouth be filled with laughter, as with Reish Lakish (Berachot 31a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:68: Likewise, when he considers that through our sins we have separated voice from speech, so that in exile she [the Shechinah] says, "I have been mute, silent" (Psalms 39:3), it is fitting that he too should bear and silence himself when they disgrace him or anger him — for the Holy One, blessed be He, bears foreigners dancing in His sanctuary because of our sins, and His great Name is profaned through us; how then can a person not bear anger or disgrace from his fellow, especially from a foreigner, as it is written (Lamentations 3:30), "let him give his cheek to the one who strikes him; let him be filled with disgrace, for the LORD does not reject forever" etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:69: And just as our sins cause the lowliness of the Shechinah, as it is said (Isaiah 26:5), "He lays it low, He humbles it" etc. "to the dust," as explained in the Gate of Awe (ch. 9) and the Gate of Repentance (ch. 7), so it is fitting for a person to be lowly and not choose lofty places. And just as her voice is low, as it is written (Isaiah 29:4), "and brought low from the earth you shall speak, and from the dust your speech shall be muffled," so it is fitting that his voice be low like a mourner's, this being (Psalms 35:14), "as one mourning for his mother I bowed down in gloom." And he should not adorn himself in fine garments except on Shabbat and festivals, for then she removes the weekday garments of exile and puts on royal garments, as explained in Tikkunim (3b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:70: Likewise, it is fitting that he not indulge in worldly pleasures on weekdays, but restrain himself as much as possible, since on weekdays the world is clothed in the lower kelipah, which is "another god," and thus one who indulges is [in effect] delighting other gods. They explained this matter in the Zohar, portion Vayakhel (207b), regarding one who fasts on Shabbat — he said his remedy is to fast one day during the week, a fast for [the violation of] the fast, and our Sages of blessed memory said, why? Because this one nullified the delight of Shabbat, so let him nullify the delight of the weekday; and if he nullifies the delight of Shabbat and indulges on a weekday, it is as though he considers another god more than he considers the Holy One, blessed be He — the supernal holy spirit of holiness that rested upon him he did not delight in and nullified from himself, but the other, weekday spirit that rests afterward upon the world, he considers and delights it; then they return and exact payment from him in this world and in the World to Come. Therefore another fast is needed on the first weekday, at the time that weekday spirit rests upon the world. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:71: Likewise, because of the reason of the Shechinah's exile, it is fitting to be distressed in one's food and not to indulge, for she in exile lacks sustenance, clothing, and conjugal rights, as is known (Tikkunei Zohar 22a-b). Likewise it is fitting to go from place to place, to be driven about in accordance with the exile of the Shechinah, just as she is exiled from place to place, as explained at the beginning of the Introduction to Tikkunim (1b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:72: Regarding the merit of one who is distressed for the sake of the Shechinah, it is said (Psalms 146:5), "fortunate is he whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the LORD his God," as explained in the Zohar (portion Vayakhel, 198a), these are his words: "whose hope [sivro]" — he does not say "his expectation" nor "his trust," but "his hope" [sivro] — do not read "shivro" [his breaking] but "sivro" [his hope] — for it pleases the righteous to break themselves, break upon break, and all for the LORD their God, as in (Psalms 44:23), "for Your sake we are killed all day long," (ibid. 69:8), "for Your sake I have borne disgrace" — along the lines of Jacob, of whom it is written (Genesis 42:1), "and Jacob saw that there was grain [shever] in Egypt" — for he saw the breaking [shever] of exile that he had in Egypt, and placed his strength in the Holy One, blessed be He; and Jacob's sons bore the breaking of exile and did not change from the secret of their fathers' faith, and the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, was habitually on their lips even in exile — and therefore it is written (Exodus 3:13), "and they say to me, what is His Name?" — for they knew Him and never forgot Him, and bore the breaking of exile for the sake of the Holy One, blessed be He; and therefore they merited redemptions, miracles, and many signs. And holy supernal beings who bear the breaking of their body from place to place for the sake of the Holy One, blessed be He, all the more so — fortunate are you to have miracles and redemptions performed for you, and you shall merit the life of the World to Come. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:73: Likewise King David, peace be upon him, was distressed for the Shechinah, saying (1 Chronicles 17:1), "behold, I dwell in a house of cedars, while the ark of the covenant of the LORD is under curtains," and he said (Psalms 132:4), "I will not give sleep to my eyes, nor slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the LORD." Along these lines a person should say, when he is at ease in his house, behold I am in tranquility and ease and secure in my house, while His Shechinah, blessed be He, is tossed about in exile because of our sins, without even a tent of curtains — this is what she says (Song of Songs 1:6), "do not look at me, that I am swarthy, that the sun has gazed upon me; my mother's sons were angry with me, they made me keeper of the vineyards," as explained regarding the exile of the Shechinah in the Zohar, portion Tazria (45b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:74: Therefore, even a wealthy person should feel distress like a poor man in his food and in the distribution among his household, and give the rest to charity, as King David, peace be upon him, said (1 Chronicles 22:14), "and behold, in my poverty I have prepared for the house of the LORD" etc. — and our Sages of blessed memory explained in the Yerushalmi of Pe'ah (4:2), "be'oni" [in my poverty] as "be'inui" [in my affliction] — that he would fast and dedicate his meal to Heaven. Similarly this is said of many people in tractate Ta'anit who used to conduct themselves this way.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:75: If a man is poor, all the more so is it fitting for him to accept sufferings with love and not be disgusted by them, and not seek stratagems to become idle from Torah and toil in worldly affairs all day in order to flee from poverty — for poverty was given to him for the atonement of his sins, and if he flees from this, the Creator does not lack the ability to exact his debt from him regardless; and it is not fitting for a servant to flee from the sufferings of his master, but to accept them with a pleasant countenance. The merit of the poor exceeds that of the wealthy — the proof being David and Solomon, for Solomon is the head of the moon at its fullness, and David at its diminishment, and David is in the secret of (Psalms 118:22), "the stone the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone," and ascends to a wondrous level; and so in the future, the cup of blessing to bless will be given only to David, as explained in Pesachim (119b). Further, regarding the merit of the righteous who are afflicted with poverty and other sufferings, they elaborated at length in portion Vayeshev (181a), which we copied in the Gate of Repentance (ch. 4).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:76: Further, regarding the merit of one who lowers himself for the sake of the Shechinah, it is explained in the Ra'aya Meheimna (portion Terumah, 158b) that he merits a soul from the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah. These are his words: but one who is poor and puts himself to death for her sake, in your own manner, Faithful Shepherd, is like a sacrifice that descends beneath you — and why? Because whoever lowers himself for the sake of the Shechinah of the Holy One, blessed be He, He descends upon him — and this is what the prophet said (Psalms 138:6), "for the LORD is high, yet He sees the lowly, and the lofty"; and further (Isaiah 57:15), "for thus says the High and Exalted One, who inhabits eternity, whose name is holy... and with the crushed and humble of spirit" — for although I am high and holy, I dwell with him who has made himself crushed and humble of spirit for the sake of My Shechinah, to raise her from her lowliness — a crown upon his head, I descend to dwell with him. And after the husband of the Shechinah [i.e., the divine presence in the form of Tiferet/Yesod] descends upon a person, she descends from upon his head and gives the place of the head to her husband, and descends to the feet of the King — and the secret of the matter is "the heavens are My throne and the earth is My footstool" (Isaiah 66:1) — for from the day a person inherits a soul comprising the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, from that hour he is called "His son." One sage said, and is he called "His son" from that very day? From where do we learn this? From this verse that David says in the book of Psalms (Psalms 2:7), "I will declare the decree: the LORD said to me, you are My son; today I have begotten you." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:77: Further, in the Ra'aya Meheimna (portion Pinchas, 239a): fortunate is one who strives, in this final exile, to know the Shechinah, to honor her with all the commandments and to bear several hardships for her sake, as it is said, the reward for a bride is [in proportion to] the hardship. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:78: One who does not support the Shechinah through his deeds — of him it is said (Isaiah 51:18), "there is none to guide her among all the sons she has borne, and none to take her by the hand among all the sons she has raised" — and especially he will be judged if it happens that the Messiah comes, as Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Zohar, portion Shemot, 7b), these are his words: Rabbi Shimon raised his hands and wept, saying, woe to whoever happens to be present at that time, and fortunate is the portion of whoever happens to be found at that time — woe to whoever happens to be there, because when the Holy One, blessed be He, comes to recall the doe [the Shechinah, imagery from Song of Songs], He will examine who stands with her, all those found with her, all the deeds of each and every one, and none will be found worthy, as it is said (Isaiah 63:5), "and I looked and there was no helper" — and how many afflictions upon afflictions for Israel! Fortunate is one who happens to be found at that time, for whoever is established in faith will merit that illumination of the King's joy. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:79: Humility — Ramban wrote in the letter he sent to his son, and I saw fit to copy it to complete the acquisition of the attribute of humility. These are his words: hear, my son, the discipline of your father, and do not forsake it. Always conduct yourself to speak gently, all your words to every person at every time, and through this you will be saved from anger, which is the evil quality that leads a person to sin. So our Sages of blessed memory said (Nedarim 22a), whoever becomes angry — all kinds of Gehinnom rule over him, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 11:10), "and remove anger from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh" — and "evil" is nothing but Gehinnom, as it is said (Proverbs 16:4), "and even the wicked for the day of evil."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:80: And when you are saved from anger, the good quality of humility, better than all good, will rise in your heart, as it is said (Proverbs 22:4), "the heel of humility is the fear of the LORD." And because of humility, the quality of fear [of Heaven] will rise in your heart, for you will always keep in mind from where you came and to where you are going, and that you are a worm and a maggot in your life, all the more so in your death, and before whom you are destined to give judgment and account — before the Glory, as it is said (1 Kings 8:27), "behold, the heavens and the heaven of heavens cannot contain You," all the more so the hearts of men — and he said (Jeremiah 23:24), "do I not fill the heavens and the earth, says the LORD." And when you consider all this, you will fear your Creator and guard yourself from sin. With these qualities you will be happy with the portion that reaches you. And when you conduct yourself with the qualities of humility, to be embarrassed before every person, and to be in awe of him and of sin, then the spirit of the Shechinah and the radiance of her glory will rest upon you, and your life and the life of the World to Come.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:81: Now, my son, know and see that whoever is proud of heart toward the creatures rebels against the kingdom of Heaven, for he adorns himself with the garment of the Omnipresent, as it is said (Psalms 93:1), "the LORD reigns, He is clothed in majesty." Why should a person's heart be proud? If because of wealth — (1 Samuel 2:7), "the LORD makes poor and makes rich." If because of honor — is it not God's, as it is said (1 Chronicles 29:12), "and wealth and honor come from before You" — so how can he adorn himself with the honor of his Maker? If he takes pride in wisdom — (Job 12:20), "He removes the speech of the trustworthy, and takes away the discernment of the elders." We find, then, that all are equal before the Omnipresent, for in His anger He humbles the proud, and by His will He raises the lowly; therefore, humble yourself and the Omnipresent will raise you up.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:82: Therefore I shall explain how you should conduct yourself with the attribute of humility to always walk in it: all your words should be gentle, your head bowed, your eyes looking down toward the ground and your heart upward, and do not look at a person's face while speaking with him. Every person should be greater than you in your eyes — if he is rich and wise, you must honor him; and if he is poor and you are richer than he, or you are wiser than he, think in your heart that you are more guilty than he and he is more innocent than you — for if he sins, it is unintentional, while you sin deliberately.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:83: In all your deeds, words, and thoughts, and at all times, think in your heart as though you stand before the Omnipresent and His Shechinah is upon you, for His glory fills the world; and your words should be with dread and awe, like a servant before his master, and be embarrassed before every person. And if a man calls you, do not answer him in a loud voice, but gently, as one standing before his master.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:84: Be always careful in the Torah that you can fulfill, and when you rise from the book, search what you have learned to see if there is something in it you can fulfill. Examine your deeds morning and evening, and through this all your days will be in repentance. Remove every extraneous matter from your heart at the time of prayer, and prepare your heart before the Omnipresent, and consider the word before it leaves your mouth — do this all the days of your life, in every single matter, and you will not sin; and through this all your deeds will be upright and your prayer pure, clean, precise, and accepted before the Omnipresent, as it is said (Psalms 10:17), "You will establish their heart, You will incline Your ear."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:85: Read this letter once a week, no less, in order to fulfill it and always walk in it after the Name, so that you succeed in all your ways and merit the World to Come that is hidden for the righteous. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:86: When a person strives to fulfill the attribute of humility as Ramban, peace be upon him, wrote in this letter, the merit of modesty will follow from it — being modest in his eating, in the privy, in marital relations, and in his other ways, and doing all of them for the sake of Heaven, because of his embarrassment before the Creator, blessed be He, who watches over him always.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:87: Regarding this matter, Ra'avad, peace be upon him, wrote a fitting matter at the end of Sha'ar HaKedushah, which I saw fit to copy, these are his words: the foremost of all fences is that a person guard his eyes from everything that is not his own, and even reduce his gazing at what is his own — and then he is called modest and shy, along the lines of what they said (Shabbat 53b) of that man whose wife's hand was amputated and he never noticed all his days, and they said of him, how modest is this man, that he never noticed his wife's condition.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:88: And if he guards his eyes, his heart is thereby guarded, and through his heart and eyes being guarded, he is entirely guarded — for through three senses in a person, the sin is completed: sight, thought, and touch. And if he has the fourth sense [hearing], it too serves touch, and is not as close to the sense of thought as sight, since sight brings immediately to the sense of the heart, and the sense of the heart brings to touch; regarding this the verse warned (Numbers 15:39), "and do not go astray after your heart and after your eyes" — and they said in the aggadah (Yerushalmi Berachot 1:5), the eye and the heart are two agents of sin. And so the sage said (Proverbs 23:26), "give me your heart, my son, and let your eyes observe my ways" — give me your heart and your eyes, and I will know that you are Mine.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:89: The very first of all first things is that a person know his Maker and recognize his Creator, and take to heart whom he serves, whom he fears, whose commandments he performs, and who has warned him — as David said to Solomon (1 Chronicles 28:9), "my son, know the God of your father and serve Him with a whole heart" — and although He is hidden from the eyes of every living being, He is found in hearts and revealed in thoughts; and every created being should know that it is neither separate from the Creator nor connected to Him, for everything connected is limited, and everything limited is created, and the Creator, blessed be He, has none of these qualities, for He is primordial before all, neither limited nor created — even though the Creator created the created being from nothing, and if it exists, it is by His will and desire, to perform His commandments and receive its reward, whether good or bad, for its own existence is neither hewn out, separated, limited, nor diminished, since it is as nothing compared to Him in its own beginning and its own likeness. And the Creator, blessed be He, is the place of His world, but His world is not His place — and the pattern of this is as the world is full of air, and everyone enters within the air and is affected by it, yet it is not visible to them. And if the verse compares man in the hand of the Creator to clay in the hand of the potter, this is to inform the ear of what it can grasp, but the parable is as far from the true intent as east is from west — for the potter who works the clay, although he makes the vessel and precedes the making of the vessel, the clay from which the vessel is made preceded the craftsman; therefore the works of the craftsman's hand are already hewn before him and separate between him and them, and diminish the sight of his eyes through their obstruction. But the Creator, blessed be He, was preceded by nothing — He created everything from nothing; therefore before Him there is nothing intervening or separating.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:90: All this the living being should take to heart, that He sees his Creator in a way his eyes do not see; and if the feet and other bodily organs sin without the heart's intent, they are unwitting in the transgression, like a blind man who does not see and eats whatever comes to his hand under presumption of permissibility, or who spits toward people without knowledge, since he did not know a person was in front of him — and it is not fitting to punish him. But one who sees what he grasps in his hand, and grasps something forbidden and eats it, or if a person stands before him and he spits in his face — is he not punished greatly for this? So too the sin of the heart and thought: when they see their Creator through the power of their intent and understanding, and if they sin against Him and are not ashamed before Him, nor embarrassed because of the honor of their Creator standing before them, and are brazen-faced before their Maker — how great is their punishment, like a man who transgresses the king's command in his very presence, whose punishment is greater and doubled compared to one who is hidden from him and transgresses his command.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:91: You, son of man, set your heart to all these matters and see their nature, and with your ears hear, and open your eyes, and see the form of your Creator standing before you, and see that He is in heaven and you are on earth, and be guarded from every evil thing. Thus far his words. And along these lines, the author of Rokeach wrote at the beginning of his book, in the root of holiness, and to avoid excessive length we have not copied his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:92: When the reader recalls what was explained in chapter 1 of the Gate of Awe regarding fearing this glorious and awesome Name (Deuteronomy 28:58), he will see with the eye of his intellect that from this fear follow modesty, shyness, humility, and piety, as is written in the Zohar (portion Naso, 145a): whoever has fear of Heaven merits humility, and whoever has humility merits piety, and whoever has fear of Heaven merits all of them — humility, as it is written (Proverbs 22:4), "the heel of humility is the fear of the LORD"; piety, as it is written (Psalms 103:17), "but the kindness of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting upon those who fear Him." We have learned, any person who has piety is called an angel of the LORD of Hosts. Thus far his words, as relevant to our purpose. And since humility and piety follow from fear, modesty and shyness are included in piety, for such a one is called an angel of the LORD of Hosts; and it is impossible to acquire these qualities except by a person keeping the supernal providence continually before him, and thinking that just as, if a person stood over him watching his every movement, he would fear to do anything disgraceful out of shame before him, so it is fitting for him to fear that the Name YHVH stands before him, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 16:8), "I have set the LORD before me always" — this being this glorious and awesome Name.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:93: Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in Song of Songs from the Zohar the matter of the Name YHVH being found even below in this world. These are his words: it is written (Song of Songs 1:4), "draw me after you, let us run" — the letters of the secret of the holy Name are engraved above and below; at the time those letters flash and rise toward other letters, all those holy camps travel in their journeys with dread and shame, since above, none of the people of the world have shame, none of them have a portion in the World to Come. Thus far his words. It is thus explicit that the letters of the Name are engraved above and below — meaning, in the supernal world and the lower world; therefore all the worlds are subjugated to do the will of their Maker when they see the letters of the great Name before them. Therefore it follows that whoever has no shame of face has no portion in the World to Come — since he is not ashamed before the King, before whom he has no portion — for according to a person's attachment of soul to the LORD, so he is bound in the supernal world; and one who is brazen-faced distances himself from the LORD because he does not fear to sin before the King who is before him, and likewise if people speak against him, he is brazen-faced to respond and is not ashamed before the Supernal King, since there is no fear of God before his eyes, and therefore he has no portion in the World to Come.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:94: To acquire this quality, persistence is needed — that every day he free himself from his affairs for at least one hour, to think of the greatness of the Name and His wonders, and place his fear before him, and through this he will be saved from sin — for one who thinks of the LORD only occasionally does not have fear truly acquired in his heart, as Rabbeinu Yonah the Pious wrote in his commentary on Proverbs, and Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him, copied his words in his commentary on the chapters, in the Mishnah "consider three things" (Avot 3:1). These are his words: the pious Rabbeinu Yonah wrote in his commentary on Proverbs (2:5), "then you shall understand the fear of the LORD, and find the knowledge of God" — two matters in knowledge of the Name, blessed be He, and he gave a parable, saying: if you passed before the king once and did not remember his form, but if you saw him again and again, you would remember that this is his form, for he is the king you saw. But another man passed before the king and remembered his form afterward, it being present in his thought, received by the imaginative faculty within him — is this one not more familiar with and knowledgeable of the king than the first? Therefore, whoever has received into his soul the knowledge of the exaltedness of the Name, blessed be He, and His fear before him, without needing to prepare his heart and arrange his thought to bring it into his mind and picture it in his soul, is the one who [truly] knows the Name, blessed be He. And I say that since a person by nature treads toward sins, he will not be saved from the transgression that comes his way unless he is crowned with the second level, which is "the knowledge of God," for the scale of his nature will tip him toward guilt; but with the remembrance of the Name, blessed be He, always before his eyes, the precious will overcome the vile. This supernal level is called in this verse "the knowledge of God," and is therefore mentioned after "fear," for it is the completion of fear. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:95: When a person persists in thinking that the Shechinah is above, he will come to purify his thoughts, and it is possible that the Tanna intended this in saying (Avot 2:1), know what is above you — a seeing eye, a hearing ear, and all your deeds are written in a book. These three things correspond to thought, speech, and action, and therefore all three were needed, and the last one alone, which encompasses all — "and all your deeds are written in a book" — would not have sufficed. "A seeing eye" corresponds to fantasies/thoughts, as it says (Jeremiah 20:12), "who sees the kidneys and the heart," and King David, peace be upon him, likewise said (Psalms 66:18), "if I had regarded iniquity in my heart" — the intent being thought. "A hearing ear" corresponds to speech — whether he spoke evil speech, or whether his prayer, his blessings, and his Torah were said without awe, as explained in Tikkunim (122a), these are his words: and whoever's voice is heard there, whether in Torah, in prayer, or in an outcry, without fear — immediately (Numbers 11:1), "and the LORD heard, and His anger burned, and the fire of the LORD burned among them." Thus far his words — the reason being, as explained there, that hearing is judgment from the side of the left. "And all your deeds are written in a book" corresponds to action, and he said "all" to include even deeds that involve neither commandment nor transgression, as Job, peace be upon him, said (Job 31:4), "does He not see my ways and count all my steps?"
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:96: In Tikkunim (142b) it is explained regarding this Mishnah that the word "mah" [what] "above" refers to the Shechinah standing above a person's head, which is called "mah," as is known. These are his words: and there are sins that are done in secret, and the angels who go with the soul, of whom it is said (Psalms 91:11), "for He shall command His angels concerning you," cannot testify about them — behold, the Shechinah testifies about them, this being what is written (Jeremiah 23:24), "if a man hides in secret places" etc. — because the Shechinah is upon his head, of whom it is said, "know what is above you — a seeing eye, a hearing ear, and all your deeds are written in a book." Thus far his words. And these designations mentioned — eye, ear, and book — are not far from being hers, as explained in the Ra'aya Meheimna (portion Pinchas, end of 256a), these are his words: she is called "eye" from the side of the right (Psalms 33:18), "behold, the eye of the LORD is toward those who fear Him," and is called "ear" from the side of the left (Daniel 9:18), "incline Your ear, my God, and hear." Thus far his words. And for the designation "book," no proofs are needed, since this is agreed upon in portion Vayakhel (200a) and in Tikkunim.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:97: When a person persists in thinking that the Shechinah is above his head, especially one who knows what the matter of the Shechinah is — some of which has already been explained in the Gate of Awe — the acquisition of humility with the conditions Ramban, peace be upon him, explained will not be far from him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:1: Now that we have explained in the preceding chapters the ways of humility, we must explain in this chapter how many qualities exist among the proud, all of which are hated before the Omnipresent, so that a person distance himself from them and complete himself in the quality of humility properly.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:2: The first quality by which the inclination misleads a person is that he arranges his clothes and curls his hair and the like, and it appears that there is no transgression in this, and he does not know that from this it draws him toward the quality of pride — for if they disgrace him, he says in his heart, "do they disgrace an honored person like me?" And in Bereshit Rabbah (22:6) our Sages of blessed memory said: Rabbi Ami said, the evil inclination does not walk to the sides but in the middle of the marketplace, and when it sees a person touching up his eyes, curling his hair, hanging by his heel [posturing], it says, "this one is mine" — why? (Proverbs 26:12), "do you see a man wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him." Rabbi Avin said, whoever pampers his inclination in his youth will eventually be dominated by it in his old age — why? (ibid. 29:21), "he who pampers his servant from youth, in the end he will become a master over him." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:3: Likewise they explained in the Zohar (portion Vayeshev, 190b) that the inclination's initial grip on a person is through the arrangement of his clothes. These are his words: (Genesis 39:12), "and she grabbed him by his garment, saying, lie with me" — "and she grabbed him by his garment" — for when the evil inclination rules over a person, it arranges and adorns his clothes for him, curls his hair — this is what is written, "and she grabbed him by his garment, saying, lie with me" — "attach yourself to me." Whoever is righteous strengthens himself against it and wages war against it — what is written? "And he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and went outside" — he abandons it and strengthens himself against it and flees from it in order to be saved from it and not let it rule over him. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:4: Further there (Zohar, portion Vayishlach, 166a-b), these are his words: Rabbi Shimon opened (Proverbs 12:9), "better a person of little esteem who has a servant, than one who honors himself and lacks bread" — this verse is said of the evil inclination, since it continually accuses people; and the evil inclination lifts up a person's heart and desire with pride, and he follows after it, curling his hair and his head, until it makes him proud and draws him to Gehinnom. But "better a person of little esteem" — one who does not follow after the evil inclination and is not proud at all, but lowers his spirit and his heart and his desire toward the Holy One, blessed be He — then that evil inclination is turned into a servant for him, unable to rule over him, and that person rules over it, as in (Genesis 4:7), "and you shall rule over it." "Than one who honors himself" — as we said, one who honors himself, curls his hair, becomes proud in spirit — "and lacks bread" — lacks faith, as in (Leviticus 21:22), "the bread of his God" etc., "the bread of their God they offer" etc. (ibid. 21:6). Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:5: Further, among the qualities of pride, he copied in the book Beit Middot, at the end of the section on proper conduct, and we shall copy all his words since they also contain qualities of humility. These are his words: fifteen things are said of a Torah scholar: pleasant in his house, pious in his manner of sitting, cunning in knowledge, sharp in his deeds, knows his own place, happy with his portion, does not take credit for himself, gives extensive answers, asks and answers, listens and answers on every point, goes to Torah scholars, and learns in order to practice.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:6: A Torah scholar must be modest in eating and drinking — he does not eat standing nor drink standing, does not wipe the plate, does not lick his fingers, does not belch before his fellow, and is modest in washing, in anointing, in his manner of dress, in his walking, in his voice, and in his good deeds.
